slides.narration: A trial balance shows what was recorded during the year. It does not yet show every expense and income that belongs to the year. Adjustments bring them in, and each one has two effects in the final accounts. In this part we study adjustments for stock, expenses, income, depreciation, goods taken by the proprietor and loss by fire, using imagined firms.

slides.heading: Why adjustments are needed
slides.body_md: The final accounts must show the income and expenses of the **year**, not only the cash that moved.

rows: The expenses of a year are set against the income of the same year
Items of the year that are unpaid or unreceived are brought in
Income and expenses are recorded when earned or incurred, not when cash moves
Outstanding, prepaid, accrued and advance items are adjusted
It records what was entered during the year
On its own it gives a wrong profit and a wrong Balance Sheet

visual.alt: Table of the matching concept, the accrual basis and the limit of the trial balance, with the result for the final accounts

slides.narration: The matching concept sets the expenses of a year against the income of the same year. The accrual basis records an item when it is earned or incurred, not when cash is paid or received. A trial balance records only what was entered, so on its own it gives a wrong profit and a wrong balance sheet. Adjustments correct this.

slides.heading: Every adjustment has two effects
slides.body_md: One effect in the Trading or Profit and Loss Account, and one in the **Balance Sheet**.

slides.narration: This chart lists the adjustments of the chapter. Read one row at a time. Each adjustment changes one item in the trading account or the profit and loss account, and one item in the balance sheet. If you record only one of the two effects, the balance sheet will not agree. Closing stock inside the trial balance is the one case with a single place.

slides.heading: Closing stock
slides.body_md: Closing stock is credited in the Trading Account only when it is given **outside** the trial balance.

rows: It is not yet in any account, so it is entered twice
The Trading Account was prepared, so only the asset remains

visual.alt: Table comparing closing stock given outside the trial balance, shown in the Trading Account and the Balance Sheet, with closing stock already inside it, shown only in the Balance Sheet

slides.narration: Closing stock given outside the trial balance has not yet been entered in any account. It is credited in the trading account and also shown as a current asset, so it appears twice. When closing stock is already in the trial balance, the trading account has been prepared, so it is shown only as a current asset in the balance sheet.

slides.heading: Quick check: closing stock
slides.body_md: Decide where the closing stock of an imagined shop appears.
slides.narration: First ask whether the closing stock is inside or outside the trial balance. Outside means it is not yet in any account. Then decide in how many statements it must appear so that both the gross profit and the balance sheet are right.

slides.heading: Outstanding and prepaid expenses
slides.body_md: An outstanding expense is **added**; a prepaid expense is **deducted**.

rows: Incurred in the year but not yet paid
Paid in the year for a later period

visual.alt: Table of the outstanding expense, incurred but unpaid, added to the expense and shown as a current liability, and the prepaid expense, paid for a later period, deducted from the expense and shown as a current asset

slides.narration: An outstanding expense is incurred in the year but not yet paid, so it is added to the expense paid, and it is a current liability. A prepaid expense is paid in the year for a later period, so it is deducted from the expense paid, and it is a current asset. The year should bear only its own cost.

slides.heading: Accrued income and income received in advance
slides.body_md: Accrued income is **added** to the income; income in advance is **deducted**.

rows: Earned in the year but not yet received
Received in the year for a later period

visual.alt: Table of accrued income, earned but not received, added to the income and shown as a current asset, and income received in advance, received for a later period, deducted from the income and shown as a current liability

slides.narration: Income is adjusted in the same way, but the other way round. Accrued income is earned in the year but not yet received, so it is added to the income, and it is a current asset. Income received in advance belongs to a later period, so it is deducted from the income, and it is a current liability.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: expenses and income of Jaya Joinery
slides.body_md: **Jaya Joinery**, an imagined firm, has wages **₹65,000**, rent **₹22,000** and interest **₹10,000** after adjustment.
bullets: Wages paid plus the outstanding wages.
Rent paid less the prepaid rent.
Interest received plus the accrued interest.

visual.alt: Adjustments of Jaya Joinery: wages paid 60,000 plus 5,000 outstanding gives 65,000; rent paid 24,000 less 2,000 prepaid gives 22,000; interest received 9,000 plus 1,000 accrued gives 10,000

slides.narration: Jaya Joinery, an imagined firm, paid wages of rupees sixty thousand, and rupees five thousand is outstanding, so rupees sixty five thousand goes to the trading account. Rent paid was rupees twenty four thousand and rupees two thousand is prepaid, so the charge is rupees twenty two thousand. Interest received was rupees nine thousand and rupees one thousand is accrued, so the income is rupees ten thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: outstanding wages
slides.body_md: Find the wages charged to the Trading Account of an imagined firm.
slides.narration: Start with the wages paid in the year. Then decide whether the unpaid wages for the last month should be added or deducted, remembering that the year must bear its own wages.

slides.heading: Depreciation
slides.body_md: **Depreciation** is the fall in the value of a fixed asset. It is an expense with no cash payment.

rows: The fall in the value of a fixed asset through use, passage of time or obsolescence
Debited as an expense of the year; no cash is paid
Deducted from the asset, which is shown at its reduced value
A given rate per cent of the book figure in the trial balance

visual.alt: Table of the rules for depreciation as an adjustment: the fall in value of a fixed asset, debited to the Profit and Loss Account, deducted from the asset in the Balance Sheet, at a given rate per cent

slides.narration: Depreciation is the fall in the value of a fixed asset through use, passage of time or obsolescence. It is debited to the profit and loss account as an expense of the year, although no cash is paid. In the balance sheet it is deducted from the asset, so the asset is shown at its reduced value. The rate is a percentage of the figure in the trial balance.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: depreciation at Hemlata Hardware
slides.body_md: Total depreciation is **₹34,000**; the assets are shown at **₹2,70,000** and **₹76,000**.

visual.alt: Depreciation of Hemlata Hardware: machinery 3,00,000 at 10 per cent gives 30,000 and is shown at 2,70,000; furniture 80,000 at 5 per cent gives 4,000 and is shown at 76,000; total depreciation 34,000

slides.narration: Hemlata Hardware, an imagined firm, has machinery of rupees three lakh, depreciated at ten per cent, which is rupees thirty thousand. Its furniture of rupees eighty thousand is depreciated at five per cent, which is rupees four thousand. The profit and loss account is debited with rupees thirty four thousand. The machinery is shown at rupees two lakh seventy thousand and the furniture at rupees seventy six thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: depreciation
slides.body_md: Find the value of machinery in the Balance Sheet of an imagined firm.
slides.narration: Work out the depreciation as a percentage of the figure in the trial balance. Then remember that the balance sheet shows the asset after depreciation has been taken off.

slides.heading: Goods withdrawn by the proprietor
slides.body_md: Goods taken for personal use come **off purchases** and go **into drawings**.

rows: The proprietor takes goods from stock for personal use, usually with no entry
The cost is deducted from purchases, which raises the gross profit
The cost is added to drawings, which reduces capital
Drawings A/c Dr. To Purchases A/c

visual.alt: Table of the treatment of goods withdrawn for personal use: deducted from purchases in the Trading Account, added to drawings and reducing capital, with the journal entry

slides.narration: When the proprietor takes goods for personal use, the goods were not bought for sale. Their cost is deducted from purchases in the trading account, so the gross profit rises. The same amount is added to drawings, which reduces capital. The entry debits drawings and credits purchases.

slides.heading: Abnormal loss of goods by fire
slides.body_md: Credit the Trading Account with the **whole loss**; charge only the **uninsured** part to profit.

rows: Credit side of the Trading Account, as the goods are not part of the cost of sales
Current asset in the Balance Sheet: insurance claim receivable
Debit side of the Profit and Loss Account as an abnormal loss

visual.alt: Table of the treatment of an abnormal loss of goods by fire: the cost credited to the Trading Account, the insurance claim a current asset, and the uninsured part debited to the Profit and Loss Account

slides.narration: When goods are destroyed by fire, the trading account is credited with their full cost, because they are not part of the cost of goods sold. The claim that the insurer admits is a current asset. Only the uninsured part, which is the loss less the claim, is debited to the profit and loss account as an abnormal loss.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a fire at Ishwar Interiors
slides.body_md: Loss **₹40,000**, claim **₹30,000**; the uninsured loss is **₹10,000**.

visual.alt: Loss of goods by fire at Ishwar Interiors: 40,000 credited to the Trading Account, 10,000 uninsured part debited to the Profit and Loss Account, and the insurance claim of 30,000 shown as a current asset

slides.narration: Ishwar Interiors, an imagined firm, lost goods costing rupees forty thousand in a fire. The insurance company admitted a claim of rupees thirty thousand. The trading account is credited with rupees forty thousand. The claim of rupees thirty thousand is a current asset. The uninsured loss of rupees ten thousand is debited to the profit and loss account.

slides.heading: Quick check: loss by fire
slides.body_md: Find the amount debited to the Profit and Loss Account for a loss of an imagined mill.
slides.narration: Remember that the claim the insurer admits is an asset, not a loss. Only the part of the loss that will not be recovered is charged to the profit and loss account.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: adjusting entries of Nisha Crafts
slides.body_md: Each adjustment is first recorded by a **journal entry**, which then carries both of its effects.

slides.narration: A firm that expects to allow discount to debtors who pay promptly may keep a provision for discount. sections.heading: 1. Why adjustments are made; the two-effects rule
sections.body_md:
The trial balance records only what was entered during the year. The **matching concept** requires the expenses of a year to be set against the income of the same year, and the **accrual basis** records an item when it is earned or incurred, not when cash is paid or received. **Adjustments** are the entries made at the end of the year, from the information given outside the trial balance, so that the final accounts show the true profit and the true position.

Every adjustment has **two effects**: one in the Trading Account or the Profit and Loss Account and one in the Balance Sheet. Because both effects are recorded, the Balance Sheet agrees. The one case with a single place is closing stock that is already in the trial balance.

key_terms.definition_md: The principle that the expenses of a period are set against the income of the same period.
The method of recording income and expenses when they are earned or incurred, whether or not cash has moved.
An entry made at the end of the year for an item that the trial balance leaves out, so that the accounts show the income and expenses of the year.

sections.heading: 2. Closing stock; outstanding and prepaid expenses; accrued and advance income
sections.body_md:
**Closing stock** given outside the trial balance is credited in the Trading Account and shown as a current asset. If it is already in the trial balance, the Trading Account has been prepared and it is shown only in the Balance Sheet.

An **outstanding expense** is added to the expense and shown as a current liability; a **prepaid expense** is deducted from the expense and shown as a current asset. **Accrued income** is added to the income and shown as a current asset; **income received in advance** is deducted from the income and shown as a current liability. A direct expense such as wages is adjusted in the Trading Account; an indirect expense such as rent in the Profit and Loss Account.

key_terms.definition_md: An expense that has been incurred in the year but not yet paid; it is a liability.
An amount paid in the year for a benefit that belongs to a later period; it is an asset.
Income that has been earned in the year but has not yet been received; it is an asset.
Income received in the year for a period that falls after it; it is a liability.

sections.heading: 3. Depreciation; goods withdrawn; abnormal loss
sections.body_md:
**Depreciation** is the fall in the value of a fixed asset through use, passage of time or obsolescence. It is debited to the Profit and Loss Account and deducted from the asset in the Balance Sheet, at the rate given on the figure in the trial balance.

**Goods withdrawn** by the proprietor for personal use are deducted from purchases in the Trading Account and added to drawings. Entry: Drawings A/c Dr. To Purchases A/c.

An **abnormal loss** of goods, such as destruction by fire, is credited to the Trading Account at the full cost of the goods. The insurance claim admitted is a current asset, and only the uninsured part is debited to the Profit and Loss Account.

sections.heading: 4. Bad debts and provisions
sections.body_md:
**Bad debts** are debts written off during the year (in the trial balance); **further bad debts** are found at the year end (an adjustment). A **provision for doubtful debts** is an amount set aside for debtors who may not pay.

The **new provision** is a percentage of the debtors after further bad debts. The charge to the Profit and Loss Account is **bad debts + further bad debts + new provision − old provision**. In the Balance Sheet, debtors are shown less further bad debts less the new provision.

A **provision for discount on debtors** is worked out on the debtors after the provision for doubtful debts; it is debited to the Profit and Loss Account (the new provision less the old, if any) and deducted from debtors.

An amount charged against profit for the debtors who may not pay, set aside before the loss occurs.
An amount charged against profit for the discount expected to be allowed to debtors who pay promptly.

sections.heading: 5. Interest on capital and drawings; manager's commission
sections.body_md:
**Interest on capital** is debited to the Profit and Loss Account and added to capital; it is a rate per cent on the opening capital. **Interest on drawings** is credited to the Profit and Loss Account and deducted from capital; it is a rate per cent on the drawings or an amount given.

**Manager's commission** is debited to the Profit and Loss Account and shown as a current liability. On the net profit **before** charging it, the commission is rate × profit ÷ 100. On the net profit **after** charging it, the commission is rate × profit ÷ (100 + rate), where the profit is the net profit before commission and after all other adjustments.

sections.heading: 6. Preparing the adjusted final accounts
sections.body_md:
Prepare the statements in the horizontal format of a sole proprietor. **Trading Account:** opening stock, purchases less returns and goods withdrawn, direct expenses with outstanding or prepaid items; net sales, closing stock and any loss of goods credited. **Profit and Loss Account:** gross profit, incomes with accrued or advance items, interest on drawings; indirect expenses with their adjustments, bad debts and provisions, depreciation, interest on capital, uninsured loss and commission.

**Balance Sheet:** capital (opening capital + interest on capital + net profit − drawings − goods withdrawn − interest on drawings), liabilities including outstanding items and commission due; assets with depreciation, further bad debts and provisions deducted, and with prepaid and accrued items and the insurance claim added. Check that both totals agree. Each adjustment is used once, and each is shown in two places.

questions.stem_md: Ishaan Traders, an imagined firm, closes its books on 31 March each year and records some expenses only when paid. Adjustments are made before its final accounts are prepared mainly because

options.text_md: the trial balance never agrees without them
the accounts must show the income and expenses that belong to the year, whether or not cash has moved
the tax authorities require every account to be adjusted
cash received and paid must be recorded in the cash book

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the accounts must show the income and expenses that belong to the year, whether or not cash has moved. The matching concept and the accrual basis require each year to carry its own income and its own expenses. A trial balance can agree and still leave out outstanding or prepaid items, tax rules do not decide the need for adjustments, and recording cash in the cash book is done during the year, not at its end.

questions.stem_md: Under the accrual basis of accounting, Sapna Stationers, an imagined shop, records rent for March 2026 in the year ended 31 March 2026 even though the landlord is paid only in April 2026, because

options.text_md: a payment made in April can never belong to the year ended in March
rent is a capital expenditure of the year
the landlord asks that the amount be recorded early
an expense belongs to the period in which it is incurred, not the period in which it is paid

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** an expense belongs to the period in which it is incurred, not the period in which it is paid. On the accrual basis an expense is recognised when it is incurred, so the rent for March belongs to the year ended in March. Cash paid later does not change the period of the expense, rent is a revenue item, and the landlord has no say in how the tenant keeps its books.

questions.stem_md: Kabir Hardware, an imagined shop, gives closing stock of ₹46,000 as an item outside its trial balance for the year ended 31 March 2026. In the final accounts the closing stock is shown

options.text_md: on the credit side of the Trading Account and as a current asset in the Balance Sheet
only on the credit side of the Trading Account
only as a current asset in the Balance Sheet
on the debit side of the Trading Account and as a current liability

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** on the credit side of the Trading Account and as a current asset in the Balance Sheet. A closing stock given outside the trial balance has not yet been entered in any account, so it is credited in the Trading Account and also shown as an asset still owned. Showing it in one place only would leave either the gross profit or the Balance Sheet wrong, and it is never a debit item or a liability.

questions.stem_md: The trial balance of Divya Dairy, an imagined firm, drawn up after the Trading Account was prepared, shows closing stock ₹38,000 on the debit side and gross profit ₹1,20,000 on the credit side. Closing stock is shown

options.text_md: on the credit side of the Trading Account and in the Balance Sheet
on the debit side of the Profit and Loss Account
only as a current asset in the Balance Sheet
as a deduction from purchases in the Trading Account

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** only as a current asset in the Balance Sheet. When closing stock already stands in the trial balance, the Trading Account has been completed and the stock has been recorded, so only the Balance Sheet is left to show it. Crediting it again would count it twice, and it is not an expense of the Profit and Loss Account.

questions.stem_md: Tara Printers, an imagined press, paid wages of ₹54,000 during the year ended 31 March 2026, and wages of ₹5,000 for March 2026 were still unpaid on that date. The amount of wages debited to the Trading Account and the treatment of the ₹5,000 are

options.text_md: ₹49,000; the ₹5,000 is shown as a current asset
₹54,000; the ₹5,000 is ignored until it is paid
₹59,000; the ₹5,000 is shown as a current liability
₹59,000; the ₹5,000 is shown as a current asset

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹59,000; the ₹5,000 is shown as a current liability. An outstanding expense is added to the amount paid, so the year bears 59,000 of wages, and the unpaid part is a liability to the workers. Deducting it, ignoring it or calling it an asset all mismatch the cost with the year or hide an amount the firm owes.

questions.stem_md: Umesh Optics, an imagined shop, paid an insurance premium of ₹18,000 on 1 January 2026 for one year. In the accounts for the year ended 31 March 2026 the amount for the period after 31 March 2026 is

options.text_md: deducted from insurance in the Profit and Loss Account and shown as a current asset
added to insurance in the Profit and Loss Account and shown as a current liability
charged in full to the Profit and Loss Account
shown as a fixed asset because insurance lasts a year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** deducted from insurance in the Profit and Loss Account and shown as a current asset. Nine of the twelve months fall after 31 March, so that part is a prepaid expense: it is taken out of the year's charge and carried forward as a current asset. Charging it in full or adding it ignores the matching of cost with period, and a prepayment is current, not fixed.

questions.stem_md: Vandana Estates, an imagined firm, earned commission of ₹6,000 for March 2026 which it received only in April 2026. At 31 March 2026 this amount is

options.text_md: income received in advance, shown as a current liability
deducted from commission received in the Profit and Loss Account
ignored, because it was not received in cash during the year
accrued income, added to commission received and shown as a current asset

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** accrued income, added to commission received and shown as a current asset. Income earned but not yet received belongs to the year in which it was earned, so it is added to the income and the amount due is a current asset. A liability and a deduction describe income received in advance, and ignoring the amount would understate the year's profit.

questions.stem_md: Yogesh Rentals, an imagined firm, has rent received of ₹30,000 in its trial balance, of which ₹4,000 is for April 2026. The treatment of the ₹4,000 in the final accounts of the year ended 31 March 2026 is

options.text_md: added to rent received and shown as a current asset
deducted from rent received and shown as a current liability
left in rent received because the cash has been received
shown as drawings of the proprietor

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** deducted from rent received and shown as a current liability. Rent for April belongs to the next year, so it is taken out of this year's income and shown as a liability, because the firm owes the tenant the use of the premises. Adding it or leaving it in would overstate the income, and it has nothing to do with drawings.

questions.stem_md: Zoya Weavers, an imagined firm, charges depreciation on its looms at the end of the year. The two effects of this adjustment are

options.text_md: a debit in the Profit and Loss Account and a deduction from the loom in the Balance Sheet
a credit in the Profit and Loss Account and an addition to the loom in the Balance Sheet
a debit in the Trading Account and a current liability
a debit in the Profit and Loss Account and a current liability

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a debit in the Profit and Loss Account and a deduction from the loom in the Balance Sheet. Depreciation is a loss of value that is an expense of the year, so it is debited to the Profit and Loss Account, and the asset is shown at its reduced value. It is neither an income nor an amount owed to anyone, so a credit, an addition or a liability does not describe it.

questions.stem_md: Aman Agencies, an imagined firm, has debtors of ₹90,000 in its trial balance and finds that a debtor owing ₹6,000 is insolvent and the whole amount cannot be recovered. In the Balance Sheet the debtors, before any provision, are shown at
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** ₹84,000. A further bad debt is written off, so it reduces the debtors, giving 84,000, and it is charged to the Profit and Loss Account. Showing 90,000 ignores the loss, 96,000 adds the bad debt, and 6,000 is only the amount written off.

questions.stem_md: Bhavik Bearings, an imagined firm, has debtors of ₹1,00,000, further bad debts of ₹4,000 and wants a provision for doubtful debts at 5 per cent of its debtors. The provision is calculated on
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹96,000. Debts already written off cannot be doubtful again, so the provision is worked out on the debtors left after the further bad debts, which is 96,000. Using 1,00,000 includes a debt that has gone, and the other figures are not the balance of good debtors.

questions.stem_md: Charu Chemicals, an imagined firm, has bad debts in its trial balance, further bad debts, an old provision for doubtful debts and a new provision. The amount charged to the Profit and Loss Account for these items is

options.text_md: bad debts + further bad debts + old provision − new provision
bad debts + new provision + old provision
further bad debts + new provision − bad debts
bad debts + further bad debts + new provision − old provision

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** bad debts + further bad debts + new provision − old provision. The year bears every bad debt written off and the provision it now needs, but the old provision was created by earlier charges and already stands as a credit, so it is set against the new one. Adding the old provision or leaving out a bad debt gives the wrong charge.

questions.stem_md: Dev Distributors, an imagined firm, has debtors of ₹80,000 after writing off further bad debts, a provision for doubtful debts of ₹4,000, and wants a provision for discount on debtors at 2 per cent. The provision for discount is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹1,520. Discount will be allowed only on the debtors who are expected to pay, so it is worked out on the debtors after the provision for doubtful debts, which is 76,000. Using 80,000 applies discount to doubtful debts, and the other bases are not the balance of good debtors.

questions.stem_md: Esha Enterprises, an imagined sole proprietorship, allows interest on the capital of its proprietor. Its two effects are

options.text_md: a credit in the Profit and Loss Account and a deduction from capital
a debit in the Trading Account and a current liability
a debit in the Profit and Loss Account and an addition to capital in the Balance Sheet
a debit in the Profit and Loss Account and a current liability

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a debit in the Profit and Loss Account and an addition to capital in the Balance Sheet. Interest on capital is treated as an expense of the business and as a gain of the proprietor, so the Profit and Loss Account is debited and the capital grows. It is not a credit item, nor a liability to an outsider.

questions.stem_md: Falguni Fabrics, an imagined firm, charges interest on the drawings of its proprietor. In the final accounts this interest is

options.text_md: debited to the Profit and Loss Account and added to capital
credited to the Profit and Loss Account and deducted from capital in the Balance Sheet
credited to the Trading Account and added to drawings
debited to the Profit and Loss Account and deducted from capital

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** credited to the Profit and Loss Account and deducted from capital in the Balance Sheet. Interest on drawings is a gain for the business and a further charge on the proprietor, so it is an income in the Profit and Loss Account and it reduces capital. A debit would treat it as an expense, and it is not part of the Trading Account.

questions.stem_md: Girish Glass, an imagined firm, pays its manager a commission of 10 per cent of net profit after charging the commission. The net profit before charging it is ₹66,000. The commission is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹6,000. When the commission is a percentage of the profit left after charging it, it is 10 over 110 of the profit before commission, which is 6,000. 6,600 is the commission on the profit before charging it, and the other figures are the profit after commission or a sum with no meaning.

questions.stem_md: At 31 March 2026 the manager of Hari Hardware, an imagined shop, has not yet been paid the commission for the year. In the Balance Sheet the commission due is shown as

options.text_md: a current asset
a current liability
a deduction from capital
a fixed asset

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a current liability. The commission has been earned by the manager and is payable within a year, so it is an amount the firm owes. It cannot be an asset, and it is an expense of the Profit and Loss Account rather than a deduction from capital.

questions.stem_md: Indu Imports, an imagined firm, shows purchases of ₹3,00,000 in its trial balance. The proprietor took goods costing ₹8,000 for personal use during the year without any entry. In the final accounts

options.text_md: purchases are shown at ₹3,08,000 and the ₹8,000 is added to drawings
purchases are shown at ₹2,92,000 and the ₹8,000 is added to capital
purchases stay at ₹3,00,000 and the ₹8,000 is a Profit and Loss expense
purchases in the Trading Account are shown at ₹2,92,000 and the ₹8,000 is added to drawings

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** purchases in the Trading Account are shown at ₹2,92,000 and the ₹8,000 is added to drawings. Goods taken by the proprietor are not goods bought for sale, so they come off purchases, giving 2,92,000, and they are drawings that reduce capital. Adding them to purchases or capital moves the entry the wrong way, and goods taken by the proprietor are not an expense of the business.

questions.stem_md: Jaya Jewellers, an imagined firm, lost goods costing ₹20,000 in a fire; the insurance company admitted a claim of ₹15,000. In the final accounts the loss is

options.text_md: credited to the Trading Account at ₹20,000, with ₹5,000 debited to the Profit and Loss Account and ₹15,000 shown as a current asset
debited to the Trading Account at ₹20,000 and ₹15,000 shown as a current liability
debited to the Profit and Loss Account at ₹20,000 with no entry in the Trading Account
credited to the Trading Account at ₹15,000 with ₹20,000 shown as an asset

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** credited to the Trading Account at ₹20,000, with ₹5,000 debited to the Profit and Loss Account and ₹15,000 shown as a current asset. The goods that were lost are taken out of the cost of the goods sold by a credit in the Trading Account at their full cost. The claim the insurer will pay is an amount receivable, and only the uninsured 5,000 is a loss of the year. The other treatments either leave the Trading Account overstated in cost or call the claim a liability.

questions.stem_md: The accountant of Kamini Kitchens, an imagined firm, forgot to record outstanding rent at the end of the year. As a result, for that year,

options.text_md: net profit is understated and current liabilities are overstated
net profit is overstated and current assets are understated
net profit is overstated and current liabilities are understated
net profit is understated and current assets are overstated

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** net profit is overstated and current liabilities are understated. Leaving out an outstanding expense makes the expenses too low, so profit is too high, and the amount the firm owes is missing from the liabilities. The other options reverse the effect on profit or attach it to assets, which this adjustment does not touch.

questions.stem_md: Lalit Laboratories, an imagined firm, charged the whole premium paid on a policy to insurance and did not record the prepaid part. For that year,

options.text_md: net profit is overstated and current assets are overstated
net profit is understated and current liabilities are overstated
net profit is understated and current assets are understated
net profit is overstated and current assets are understated

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** net profit is understated and current assets are understated. Charging the prepaid part to the year makes the expense too high, so profit is too low, and the asset that the prepayment represents is missing from the Balance Sheet. A liability is not involved, and profit cannot be overstated by an extra charge.

questions.stem_md: Manish Motors, an imagined firm, did not charge depreciation on its delivery van for the year. The Balance Sheet then shows

options.text_md: net profit overstated and the van overstated
net profit understated and the van overstated
net profit overstated and the van understated
net profit understated and the van understated

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** net profit overstated and the van overstated. Without the charge the expenses are too low, so profit is too high, and the van is still shown at its old value, which is too high. An understated profit or an understated van would need an extra charge, not a missing one.

questions.stem_md: Neha Nurseries, an imagined firm, has outstanding rent of ₹3,000 at the end of the year. Where does the outstanding rent appear in the final accounts?

options.text_md: in the Trading Account, as a credit, and as a current asset
only in the Balance Sheet, as a current asset
only in the Profit and Loss Account, as an income
in the Profit and Loss Account, added to rent, and as a current liability in the Balance Sheet

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** in the Profit and Loss Account, added to rent, and as a current liability in the Balance Sheet. An adjustment is shown in two places: the expense is increased in the Profit and Loss Account and the unpaid amount is a liability in the Balance Sheet. Rent is not a trading item, and an amount owed is never an asset or an income.

questions.stem_md: Omkar Organics, an imagined firm, makes several adjustments at the end of the year. Which one of them changes the gross profit and not only the net profit?

options.text_md: depreciation on machinery
goods withdrawn by the proprietor for personal use
interest on capital
a provision for doubtful debts

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** goods withdrawn by the proprietor for personal use. Goods withdrawn are deducted from purchases in the Trading Account, so they raise the gross profit. Depreciation, interest on capital and a provision for doubtful debts all go to the Profit and Loss Account and change the net profit only.

questions.stem_md: Pooja Plastics, an imagined firm, has furniture of ₹60,000 in its trial balance and charges depreciation at 10 per cent for the year. In the Balance Sheet the furniture is shown at
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹54,000. Depreciation of 6,000 is deducted from the furniture, so it is shown at 54,000. Showing 60,000 ignores the charge, 66,000 adds it, and 6,000 is the charge itself, not the value of the furniture.

questions.stem_md: Qamar Quilts, an imagined firm, has interest received of ₹8,000 in its trial balance and interest accrued but not received of ₹1,500. The interest credited to the Profit and Loss Account is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** ₹9,500. Accrued income is added to the income received, so the year is credited with 9,500. Subtracting it treats it as income in advance, 8,000 leaves it out, and 1,500 is only the accrued part.

questions.stem_md:

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** A prepaid expense is a benefit the firm has paid for and not yet used, so it is a current asset, and the expense of the year is reduced by it.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.stem_md: Rohit Roofing, an imagined firm, paid wages of ₹48,000 during the year ended 31 March 2026. Wages of ₹6,000 for March 2026 remained unpaid on that date. Find the wages to be charged to the Trading Account for the year (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: Outstanding wages are added to the wages paid: 48,000 + 6,000 = ₹54,000. The ₹6,000 is shown as a current liability in the Balance Sheet.

questions.stem_md: Sunil Stores, an imagined shop, paid an insurance premium of ₹24,000 on 1 October 2025 for twelve months. Find the insurance to be charged to the Profit and Loss Account for the year ended 31 March 2026 (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: Only six months, October 2025 to March 2026, fall in the year: 24,000 × 6 ÷ 12 = ₹12,000. The remaining ₹12,000 is a prepaid expense, shown as a current asset.

questions.stem_md: Tanvi Tailors, an imagined firm, has machinery of ₹2,40,000 in its trial balance on 31 March 2026 and charges depreciation at 15 per cent for the year. Find the value at which the machinery is shown in the Balance Sheet (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: Depreciation = 15 per cent of 2,40,000 = ₹36,000. Value in the Balance Sheet = 2,40,000 − 36,000 = ₹2,04,000.

questions.stem_md: Usha Umbrellas, an imagined firm, has debtors of ₹80,000 and bad debts of ₹2,000 in its trial balance on 31 March 2026. Further bad debts are ₹3,000, and a provision for doubtful debts of 5 per cent on the debtors is to be created; there is no old provision. Find the amount charged to the Profit and Loss Account for bad debts and the provision (in ₹).

Vimal Vessels, an imagined firm, has debtors of ₹90,000 on 31 March 2026. Further bad debts are ₹2,000. A provision for doubtful debts at 5 per cent and then a provision for discount on debtors at 2 per cent are to be made. Find the provision for discount on debtors (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: Debtors after further bad debts: 88,000. Provision for doubtful debts = 5 per cent = 4,400, leaving 83,600. Provision for discount = 2 per cent of 83,600 = ₹1,672.

questions.stem_md: The net profit of Sohan Sports, an imagined firm, for the year ended 31 March 2026 is ₹1,32,000 before charging the manager's commission. The manager is entitled to 10 per cent of the net profit after charging the commission. Find the manager's commission (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: Commission = 1,32,000 × 10 ÷ 110 = ₹12,000. Net profit after the commission = 1,32,000 − 12,000 = 1,20,000, and 10 per cent of that is 12,000, the same amount.

questions.stem_md: Meghna Mills, an imagined firm, lost goods costing ₹36,000 in a fire on 12 March 2026. The insurance company admitted a claim of ₹28,000. Find the amount debited to the Profit and Loss Account for the loss (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: The Trading Account is credited with the whole loss of 36,000. The claim of 28,000 is a current asset. The uninsured loss = 36,000 − 28,000 = ₹8,000 is debited to the Profit and Loss Account.

questions.stem_md: Nalini Novelties, an imagined firm, has debtors of ₹1,50,000 on 31 March 2026. Further bad debts are ₹6,000 and a provision for doubtful debts of 4 per cent is to be created on the remaining debtors. Find the amount at which the debtors are shown in the Balance Sheet (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: Debtors after further bad debts: 1,50,000 − 6,000 = 1,44,000. Provision = 4 per cent = 5,760. Debtors shown = 1,44,000 − 5,760 = ₹1,38,240.

questions.stem_md: Omprakash Oils, an imagined firm, began the year ended 31 March 2026 with capital of ₹2,40,000. It allows interest on capital at 6 per cent and charges interest on drawings at 5 per cent. Drawings were ₹36,000, and the net profit for the year, after all adjustments including both interests, is ₹60,000. Find the capital shown in the Balance Sheet (in ₹).

questions.stem_md: What is a provision for doubtful debts? Why does Waheed Wholesalers, an imagined firm, create it at the end of the year?
questions.solution_md: Meaning and the matching reason.

answer.model_answer_md: A provision for doubtful debts is an amount set aside out of profit for debtors who may not pay. It is created because the loss from such debts is likely to arise from this year's sales, so the matching concept requires it to be charged to this year's profit.

questions.stem_md: A manager of Xena Exports, an imagined firm, is paid a commission on net profit. Distinguish the commission worked out on the net profit before charging it from the commission on the net profit after charging it, with the formula for each.
